claim: Protein function arises from a poorly understood pattern of energetic interactions between amino acid residues.
source: Protein function arises from a poorly understood pattern of energetic interactions between amino acid residues.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field, presented as established understanding.

claim: Deep coupling scan (DCS) enables measurement of many thousands of pairwise amino acid couplings in several homologs of a protein family.
source: Here, we extend deep-mutation technologies to enable measurement of many thousands of pairwise amino acid couplings in several homologs of a protein family – a deep coupling scan (DCS).
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of the DCS method, with experimental data supporting this capability.

claim: Cooperative interactions between residues are loaded in a sparse, evolutionarily conserved, spatially contiguous network of amino acids.
source: The data show that cooperative interactions between residues are loaded in a sparse, evolutionarily conserved, spatially contiguous network of amino acids.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental DCS data presented in the manuscript showing patterns of amino acid coupling.

claim: The pattern of amino acid coupling is quantitatively captured in the coevolution of amino acid positions, especially as indicated by statistical coupling analysis (SCA).
source: The pattern of amino acid coupling is quantitatively captured in the coevolution of amino acid positions, especially as indicated by the statistical coupling analysis (SCA), providing experimental confirmation of the key tenets of this method.
evidence: The manuscript presents correlation analysis between experimental coupling data and SCA predictions (Figure 6).

claim: The basic biological properties of proteins (structure, function, and evolvability) arise from the pattern of energetic interactions between amino acid residues.
source: The basic biological properties of proteins -- structure, function, and evolvability -- arise from the pattern of energetic interactions between amino acid residues (Anfinsen, 1973; Gregoret and Sauer, 1993; Luque et al., 2002; Starr and Thornton, 2016; Weinreich et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to established literature in the field.

claim: Amino acids act heterogeneously and cooperatively in contributing to protein fitness.
source: Amino acids act heterogeneously and cooperatively in contributing to protein fitness, properties that are not simple, intuitive functions of the positions of atoms in atomic structures (Alber et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established understanding in the field.

claim: The thermodynamic double mutant cycle (TDMC) is an experimental approach for deducing the pattern of interactions between amino acid residues.
source: In principle, an experimental approach for deducing the pattern of interactions between amino acid residues is the thermodynamic double mutant cycle (Carter et al., 1984; Hidalgo and MacKinnon, 1995; Horovitz and Fersht, 1990) (TDMC, Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to established methods and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A complete pairwise analysis of a PDZ domain comprising all possible amino acid substitutions involves making and measuring nearly two million mutations.
source: For even a small protein interaction module such as the PDZ domain (~100 residues, Figure 1B) (Hung and Sheng, 2002), a complete pairwise analysis comprising all possible amino acid substitutions at each position involves making and quantitatively measuring the equilibrium energetic effect of nearly two million mutations.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the combinatorial complexity of mutations in a protein of known size.

claim: A bacterial two-hybrid (BTH) assay for ligand-binding coupled to next-generation sequencing enables high-throughput, robust, quantitative measurement of many thousands of mutations in a single experiment.
source: In the PDZ domain, a bacterial two-hybrid (BTH) assay for ligand-binding coupled to next-generation sequencing enables high-throughput, robust, quantitative measurement of many thousands of mutations in a single experiment – a 'deep mutational scan' (Fowler and Fields, 2014; McLaughlin et al., 2012; Raman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work and the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The throughput of DCS is so high that it enables the study of double mutant cycles in several homologs of a protein family in a single experiment.
source: Indeed, the throughput of DCS is so high that it enables the study of double mutant cycles in several homologs of a protein family in a single experiment.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental data collected for five PDZ homologs as described in the manuscript.

claim: Independent trials of the DCS experiment show excellent reproducibility.
source: Independent trials of this experiment show excellent reproducibility (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and propagation of errors suggests an average experimental error in determining binding free energies of ~0.3 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is supported by reproducibility data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: 56,694 double mutant cycles (87% of total) were collected for the α2 helix for all five homologs, with an average of 315 cycles per position pair per homolog.
source: Filtering for sequencing quality and counting statistics, we were able to practically collect 56,694 double mutant cycles (87% of total) for the α2 helix for all five homologs, with an average of 315 cycles per position pair per homolog (Table 1).
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental data collection as detailed in Table 1.

claim: Distributions of thermodynamic coupling energies follow single or double-Gaussian distributions.
source: In general, the data follow single or double-Gaussian distributions (Figures 2 and 3, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–5, and see Materials and methods), with most distributions centered close to zero and with just a few position pairs displaying two distinct populations.
evidence: This is supported by the distribution plots shown in Figures 2, 3, and supplementary figures.

claim: Every mutation is associated with the full range of coupling energies.
source: In general, every mutation is associated with the full range of coupling energies, and the distributions of couplings are not immediately obvious from known chemical properties of amino acids or secondary structure propensities (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations to glycine and proline show a broad range of coupling energies not unlike other mutations.
source: For example, mutations to glycine and proline might be expected to disrupt the α2 helix, and cause global large couplings with every other mutation, but in fact we find that these substitutions show a broad range of coupling energies not unlike other mutations.
evidence: This is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations act as random perturbations to the native state of proteins, with the population-weighted mean of the distribution of coupling energies for each position pair providing the best empirical estimate of the native interaction.
source: The data suggest that as an ensemble, mutations act as random perturbations to the native state of proteins, with the population-weighted mean of the distribution of coupling energies for each position pair (Figures 2–3, dashed lines) providing the best empirical estimate of the native interaction between amino acids through mutagenesis.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data patterns shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: The spread of the distributions of coupling energies is large, generally exceeding the estimated magnitude of the native interactions.
source: First, the spread of the distributions is large, generally exceeding the estimated magnitude of the native interactions (Figures 2–3).
evidence: This is observed in the distribution plots shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: Traditional mutant cycle studies carried out with specific choices of mutations are more likely to reflect the choice of mutations rather than the native interaction.
source: This means (1) that traditional mutant cycle studies carried out with specific choices of mutations are more likely to just reflect the choice of mutations rather than the native interaction, and (2) that the only way to obtain good estimates of the native interaction between residues is to average over the effect of many double mutant cycles per position pair.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that coupling energy distributions are broad.

claim: The BTH/sequencing approach displays reproducibility such that it is possible to detect coupling energies with an accuracy on par with the best biochemical assays.
source: Second, we find that the BTH/sequencing approach displays such good reproducibility that it is possible to detect coupling energies with an accuracy that is on par with the best biochemical assays. For example, the average standard deviation in mean coupling energies for position pairs over four independent experimental replicates in PSD95pdz3 is ~0.06 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is supported by the reproducibility data from independent experimental replicates.

claim: The uni/bi-modal character of distributions of thermodynamic mutant cycle couplings is found in all the individual PDZ homologs tested, the average over homologs, and in an unrelated protein (GB1).
source: The uni/bi-modal character of distributions of thermodynamic mutant cycle couplings is striking in two respects. First is the generality. The same distribution shapes are found in all the individual PDZ homologs tested (Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4), the average over homologs (Figure 3), and even for DCS in an unrelated protein (GB1, Figure 2—figure supplement 5 [Olson et al., 2014]).
evidence: This is supported by distribution data shown across multiple figures for different proteins.

claim: The same position-pairs in every PDZ homolog display mean coupling energies close to zero and the same few position pairs display bimodal or non-zero means.
source: Second, the distribution shapes seem to be defined more by position, rather than by the character of mutations. For example, with a few exceptions, the same position-pairs in every PDZ homolog display mean coupling energies close to zero and the same few position pairs display bimodal or non-zero means (compare Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4, and see Figure 3).
evidence: This is observed by comparing coupling data across homologs in Figures 2, 3, and supplements.

claim: The observed free energy of ligand binding arises from a cooperative internal equilibrium between two distinct conformational states of a protein.
source: A simple mechanistic model for mutant cycle distributions is that the observed free energy of ligand binding arises from a cooperative internal equilibrium between two distinct conformational states of a protein (labeled 0 and 1, Figure 4A), with just a few sites defining this equilibrium.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed to explain the observed distribution patterns, illustrated in Figure 4A.

claim: A cooperative two-state internal equilibrium involving the α2 helix has been experimentally observed in a PDZ domain.
source: Nevertheless, we note that a cooperative two-state internal equilibrium involving the α2 helix has been experimentally observed in a PDZ domain, and is part of an allosteric regulatory mechanism controlling ligand binding (Mishra et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior experimental work.

claim: Bimodality in mutational couplings in diverse PDZ homologs and in the GB1 protein suggests that a two-state internal equilibrium may be a common feature of many proteins.
source: The findings here of bimodality in mutational couplings in diverse PDZ homologs and in the GB1 protein suggests that a two-state internal equilibrium may be a common feature of many proteins.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed patterns across multiple proteins.

claim: Each PDZ domain displays variations in the pattern and strength of amino acid energetic couplings, but also includes a set of evolutionarily conserved couplings at a few positions.
source: Thus, each PDZ domain displays variations in the pattern and strength of amino acid energetic couplings, but also includes a set of evolutionarily conserved couplings at a few positions.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of coupling matrices across homologs shown in Figure 5A-E.

claim: All pairwise interactions between positions 1, 4, 5, and 8 show a systematic pattern of energetic coupling in all homologs tested.
source: In contrast, all pairwise interactions between positions 1, 4, 5, and 8 show a systematic pattern of energetic coupling in all homologs tested.
evidence: This is observed in the coupling matrices shown in Figure 5A-E.

claim: Positions 1, 4, 5, and 8 comprise a cooperative network of functional residues in the PDZ domain family.
source: This analysis reinforces the result that positions 1, 4, 5, and 8 comprise a cooperative network of functional residues in the PDZ domain family, and the remainder, even if in direct contact with each other or with ligand, contribute less and interact idiosyncratically or not at all.
evidence: This is supported by the homolog-averaged coupling data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The conserved couplings form a chain of physically contiguous residues in the tertiary structure that both contact (1, 5, 8) and do not contact (4) the ligand.
source: The conserved couplings form a chain of physically contiguous residues in the tertiary structure that both contact (1, 5, 8) and do not contact (4) the ligand (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is shown in the structural representation in Figure 5H.

claim: Position 4 is part of the distributed allosteric regulatory mechanism in the InaD PDZ domain.
source: Interestingly, position 4 is part of the distributed allosteric regulatory mechanism in the InaD PDZ domain discussed above (Mishra et al., 2007), providing a biological role for its energetic connectivity with binding pocket residues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work on the InaD PDZ domain.

claim: The pattern of direct contacts that define the protein structure and the pattern of cooperative amino acid interactions that define protein function are not the same.
source: The salient point that emerges from these data is that the pattern of direct contacts that define the protein structure and the pattern of cooperative amino acid interactions that define protein function are not the same.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison of contact patterns (Figure 5F) with coupling patterns (Figure 5G).

claim: Statistical coevolution represents a kind of combined averaging over mutations and homologs.
source: Statistical coevolution also represents a kind of combined averaging over mutations and homologs, and if experimentally verified, would (unlike deep mutational studies) represent a scalable and general approach for learning the architecture of amino acid interactions underlying function in a protein.
evidence: This is a conceptual statement about the nature of coevolution analysis.

claim: SCA reveals a sparse internal organization in the PDZ domain family in which most positions evolve in a nearly independent manner and a few (~20%) are engaged in a pattern of mutual coevolution.
source: In the PDZ domain family (~1600 sequences, pySCA6.0 [Rivoire et al., 2016]), SCA reveals a sparse internal organization in which most positions evolve in a nearly independent manner and a few (~20%) are engaged in a pattern of mutual coevolution (Halabi et al., 2009; Lockless and Ranganathan, 1999; Rivoire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by SCA analysis and citations to prior work.

claim: The SCA predictions hold for individual homologs.
source: The predictions also hold for individual homologs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), consistent with the premise that the essential physical constraints underlying function are deeply conserved.
evidence: This is supported by correlation data for individual homologs shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The goodness of SCA prediction depends strongly on both conservation-weighting and correlation.
source: Importantly, the goodness of prediction depends strongly on both of the basic tenets that underlie the SCA method – conservation-weighting (Figure 6E–F) and correlation (Figure 6G–H) (Rivoire et al., 2016).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ablation analysis shown in Figure 6E-H.

claim: Groups of coevolving positions form physically connected networks of amino acids (termed protein 'sectors') that link the main functional site to distantly positioned allosteric sites.
source: A basic result of the SCA method is that groups of coevolving positions form physically connected networks of amino acids (termed protein 'sectors') that link the main functional site to distantly positioned allosteric sites (Halabi et al., 2009; Lockless and Ranganathan, 1999; Süel et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on SCA and protein sectors.

claim: In the PDZ domain, the protein sector represents a chain of amino acids that links the β2-β3 loop with the α1-β4 surface through the binding pocket and the buried α1 helix.
source: Indeed, in the PDZ domain, the protein sector represents a chain of amino acids the links the β2-β3 loop with the α1-β4 surface through the binding pocket and the buried α1 helix (spheres and surface, Figure 7).
evidence: This is shown in the structural representation in Figure 7.

claim: The four positions experimentally identified as a cooperative unit (1, 4, 5, 8) represent the portion of the α2 helix that is contained in the protein sector.
source: The four positions experimentally identified here as a cooperative unit (1, 4, 5, 8, red spheres, Figure 7) represent the portion of the α2 helix that is contained in the protein sector.
evidence: This is shown by comparison of experimental coupling data with sector positions in Figure 7.

claim: The best predictive power of DCA comes from one moderately-sized structure-based sequence alignment rather than from the largest publicly available alignments.
source: Interestingly, the best predictive power comes from one moderately-sized structure-based sequence alignment (Figure 8C) rather than from the largest publicly available alignments (Figure 8D–E).
evidence: This is shown by comparing correlation coefficients across different alignments in Figures 8C-E.

claim: DCA is quite sensitive to alignment size, with random sub-samplings of the best performing alignment producing models with variable quality.
source: Due to inclusion of many unconserved correlations, DCA is quite sensitive to alignment size, with random sub-samplings of the best performing alignment producing models with variable quality in terms of predicting the data (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by sub-sampling analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The many non-contact pairwise couplings in the DCA model contribute significantly to prediction of function.
source: Thus, the many non-contact pairwise couplings in the DCA model, which represent noise from the point of view of structure prediction, contribute significantly to prediction of function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the scrambling experiment comparing Figure 8C with Figure 8F.

claim: The SCA coevolution matrix provides an improved prediction of experimental couplings compared to DCA, including long-range ones.
source: Furthermore, the finding that the SCA coevolution matrix provides an improved prediction of experimental couplings (Figure 8B–D), including long-range ones (e.g. 1-8, Figure 6A) argues that information about allosteric energetic interactions are contained in the statistics of alignments and are therefore part of the total evolutionary constraint.
evidence: This is supported by comparing correlation coefficients between SCA (Figure 6) and DCA (Figure 8) predictions.

claim: Averaging thermodynamic couplings over many pairs of mutations provides an estimate of the native interactions between amino acids.
source: We show that averaging thermodynamic couplings over many pairs of mutations provides an estimate of the native interactions between amino acids, and exposes an architecture in which most pairs of amino acids are uncoupled and a few significantly interact to make a cooperative network underlying function.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the distribution analysis shown in Figures 2-3.

claim: Most pairs of amino acids are uncoupled and a few significantly interact to make a cooperative network underlying function.
source: We show that averaging thermodynamic couplings over many pairs of mutations provides an estimate of the native interactions between amino acids, and exposes an architecture in which most pairs of amino acids are uncoupled and a few significantly interact to make a cooperative network underlying function.
evidence: This is shown by the sparse pattern of significant couplings in Figure 5G.

claim: Averaging over homologs refines the pattern of cooperativity, revealing an evolutionarily conserved network of cooperative amino acid interactions.
source: Further averaging over homologs refines the pattern of cooperativity, revealing an evolutionarily conserved network of cooperative amino acid interactions that includes both direct and allosteric influences on ligand binding.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing individual homolog data (Figure 5A-E) with homolog-averaged data (Figure 5G).

claim: A full understanding of proteins requires inference of both direct local structural contacts and the network of cooperative interactions that underlies function.
source: This pattern is distinct from the pattern of local contacts between residues that defines secondary structure elements and the tertiary structure, indicating that a full understanding of proteins requires inference of both direct local structural contacts and the network of cooperative interactions that underlies function.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that contact patterns (Figure 5F) differ from coupling patterns (Figure 5G).

claim: DCS serves mainly to provide a critical benchmark to explore other strategies that have the generality and scalability to learn the global pattern of amino acid interactions.
source: In this regard, we suggest that DCS serves mainly to provide a critical benchmark to explore other strategies that have the generality and scalability to learn the global pattern.
evidence: This is a statement about the role and purpose of the DCS method in the broader context.

claim: Two different approaches for coevolution – DCA and SCA – effectively report the experimentally determined pattern of structural contacts and functional couplings, respectively.
source: In fact, we show that two different approaches for coevolution – DCA and SCA – effectively report the experimentally determined pattern of structural contacts and functional couplings, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the correlation analyses shown in Figures 6 and 8.

claim: Introduction of new molecular interactions at sector edges has been shown to be a route to engineering new allosteric control in protein molecules.
source: Consistent with this, introduction of new molecular interactions at sector edges has been shown to be a route to engineering new allosteric control in protein molecules (Lee et al., 2008; Reynolds et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on protein engineering.

claim: DCA successfully predicts contacts in protein structures in the top couplings, but in its current form, does not appear to capture the cooperative constraints that underlie protein function well.
source: DCA successfully predicts contacts in protein structures in the top couplings, but in its current form, does not appear to capture the cooperative constraints that underlie protein function well.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative analysis of DCA and SCA predictions against experimental data.

claim: SCA does not predict direct structural contacts well, but instead seems to accurately capture the energetic couplings that contribute to protein function.
source: In contrast, SCA does not predict direct structural contacts well, but instead seems to accurately capture the energetic couplings that contribute to protein function.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparative analysis of SCA predictions against experimental coupling data.

claim: DCA and SCA sample different parts of the information contained in a sequence alignment.
source: As explained previously, these two approaches sample different parts of the information contained in a sequence alignment (Cocco et al., 2013; Rivoire, 2013), and therefore are not mutually incompatible.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior theoretical work.

claim: With a sufficient ensemble of sequences comprising the evolutionary history of a protein family and further technical advancements, the pattern of relevant amino acid interactions can be inferred without any experiments.
source: Indeed, the remarkable implication is that with a sufficient ensemble of sequences comprising the evolutionary history of a protein family and the further technical advancements suggested above, the pattern of relevant amino acid interactions can be inferred without any experiments.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion drawn from the success of coevolution methods in predicting experimental data.

claim: Ligand binding induces transcription of the reporter gene, which enables growth in the presence of the antibiotic chloramphenicol.
source: Ligand binding induces transcription of the reporter gene, which enables growth in the presence of the antibiotic chloramphenicol.
evidence: This describes the mechanism of the bacterial two-hybrid assay shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The assay is remarkably reproducible, with >95% of values with a variance less than 0.31 kcal/mol.
source: The data show that the assay is remarkably reproducible, with >95% of values with a variance less than 0.31 kcal/mol.
evidence: This is shown by the reproducibility data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The five PDZ homologs used in this study have 33% average sequence identity.
source: Structural overlay of the five PDZ homologs used in this study (PSD95pdz3 (1BE9, white), PSD95pdz2 (1QLC, orange), ZO1pdz (2RRM, yellow), Shank3pdz (5IZU, gray), and Syntrophinpdz (1Z86, blue)), emphasizing the conserved αβ-fold architecture of these sequence-diverse proteins (33% average identity, Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption for Figure 1B and supported by Table 1.

claim: Essentially all measurements fall within the independently validated range of the assay.
source: The red lines indicate the independently validated range of the assay (Figure 1—figure supplement 1); essentially all measurements fall within this range.
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1D-E with reference to validation data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Growth at 25°C appears to represent an optimum in maximizing dynamic range while also focusing assay sensitivity to binding affinity rather than protein stability.
source: Growth at 25°C appears to represent an optimum in maximizing dynamic range whole also focusing assay sensitivity to binding affinity rather than protein stability.
evidence: This is a statement about optimization of experimental conditions.
